questions.subject: Physics
questions.text: The S.I. unit of electric current is the
questions.explanation: The ampere (A) is one of the seven base S.I. units, defined as the base unit of electric current.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.text: Which instrument is used to measure the diameter of a thin wire to the nearest 0.01 mm?
questions.explanation: The micrometer screw gauge has a much finer scale (typically 0.01 mm precision) than Vernier calipers (0.01 cm), making it suited to very thin objects like wires.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.text: Vernier calipers are typically used to measure internal and external diameters to the nearest
questions.explanation: Vernier calipers commonly have a precision of 0.01 cm (0.1 mm), useful for measuring lengths, diameters, and depths more precisely than a metre rule.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.text: The number 0.004530 expressed to 3 significant figures is
questions.explanation: Counting significant figures from the first non-zero digit: 4, 5, 3 are the first three significant figures, giving 0.00453.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.text: Which of the following is a derived S.I. unit?
questions.explanation: The newton is derived from the base units kg, m, and s (N = kg m/s2), unlike the metre, kilogram, and kelvin, which are base units.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.text: The dimension of density (mass/volume) is
questions.explanation: Density = mass/volume = M / L3 = ML-3, since volume has dimension L3 (length cubed).

questions.subject: Physics
questions.text: A scalar quantity is one that has
questions.explanation: Scalars, such as mass, distance, and speed, are fully described by a magnitude alone, unlike vectors, which also require a direction.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.text: Which of the following is a vector quantity?
questions.explanation: Displacement has both magnitude and a specified direction from a starting point, making it a vector, unlike mass, time, and energy, which are scalars.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.text: Two forces of 3 N and 4 N act at right angles to each other on an object. What is the magnitude of the resultant force?
questions.explanation: Using Pythagoras' theorem for perpendicular vectors: resultant = sqrt(3^2 + 4^2) = sqrt(9+16) = sqrt(25) = 5 N.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.text: The horizontal component of a force of 10 N acting at 30 degrees to the horizontal is
questions.explanation: The horizontal component of a vector is found by multiplying its magnitude by the cosine of the angle it makes with the horizontal axis.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.text: A boat heads directly across a river with its own velocity, while the river current pushes it downstream. The boat's resultant velocity relative to the bank is found by
options: simple arithmetic subtraction of the two speeds
vector addition of the boat's velocity and the river's velocity
the boat's velocity alone, ignoring the current
questions.explanation: Relative velocity problems are solved by vector addition, combining the boat's velocity relative to water with the water's velocity relative to the bank.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.text: Which method can be used to find the resultant of two vectors acting at an angle to each other?
options: The parallelogram law of vector addition
questions.explanation: The parallelogram law states that two vectors can be represented as adjacent sides of a parallelogram, with the resultant being the diagonal from their common point.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.text: An object starts from rest and accelerates uniformly at 2 m/s2 for 5 seconds. What is its final velocity?
questions.explanation: Using v = u + at: v = 0 + (2 x 5) = 10 m/s, since the object starts from rest (u = 0).

questions.subject: Physics
questions.text: A car travels at a constant velocity of 20 m/s for 10 seconds. What distance does it cover?
questions.explanation: Distance = velocity x time = 20 x 10 = 200 m, since the velocity is constant (zero acceleration).

questions.subject: Physics
questions.text: A body moving with uniform acceleration covers a distance given by s = ut + 1/2 at^2. If u = 0, a = 4 m/s2, and t = 3 s, what is s?

questions.subject: Physics
questions.text: Newton's First Law of Motion states that a body will remain at rest or in uniform motion in a straight line unless
options: acted upon by an external unbalanced force
questions.explanation: This is the law of inertia: an object's state of motion changes only when a net external force acts on it.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.text: Newton's Second Law of Motion is mathematically expressed as
questions.explanation: Newton's Second Law states that force equals the rate of change of momentum, which for constant mass simplifies to F = ma (mass x acceleration).

questions.subject: Physics
questions.text: A resultant force of 20 N acts on a mass of 4 kg. What acceleration does it produce?
questions.explanation: Using F = ma: a = F/m = 20/4 = 5 m/s2.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.text: Newton's Third Law of Motion states that
options: an object at rest stays at rest unless acted upon
momentum is always conserved in a closed system
for every action, there is an equal and opposite reaction
questions.explanation: Newton's Third Law describes the mutual nature of forces: whenever one body exerts a force on another, the second exerts an equal and opposite force back on the first.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.text: The momentum of a body is defined as the product of its
questions.explanation: Momentum (p) = mass (m) x velocity (v), a vector quantity with the same direction as the velocity.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.text: A 2 kg object moving at 3 m/s collides and comes to rest in 0.5 s. What is the impulse delivered to it?
questions.explanation: Impulse = change in momentum = m(v-u) = 2(0-3) in magnitude = 6 Ns, the momentum lost by the object during the collision.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.text: In Simple Harmonic Motion (SHM), the acceleration of the oscillating body is always
options: directly proportional to its displacement from equilibrium and directed towards it
questions.explanation: SHM is defined by acceleration a = -omega^2 x, proportional to displacement x but directed opposite to it, always pulling the body back to equilibrium.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.text: A body undergoing projectile motion (ignoring air resistance) experiences which acceleration in the horizontal direction?
options: Acceleration equal to the initial vertical velocity
questions.explanation: In projectile motion, gravity acts only vertically, so the horizontal component of velocity remains constant throughout the flight (zero horizontal acceleration).

questions.subject: Physics
questions.text: The time taken for a projectile to reach maximum height depends on its
options: angle of projection only, independent of speed
initial vertical component of velocity and the acceleration due to gravity
questions.explanation: Time to maximum height, t = u_vertical / g, depends on the vertical component of the initial velocity and the local gravitational acceleration.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.text: Newton's Law of Universal Gravitation states that the gravitational force between two masses is
options: inversely proportional to the product of their masses
directly proportional to the product of their masses and inversely proportional to the square of the distance between them
independent of the distance between them
directly proportional to the distance between them
questions.explanation: F = Gm1m2/r^2, showing gravitational attraction increases with mass and decreases sharply (inverse square) with increasing separation.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.text: The acceleration due to gravity, g, on the Earth's surface is approximately
questions.explanation: The standard value for acceleration due to gravity near the Earth's surface is approximately 9.8 m/s2 (sometimes approximated as 10 m/s2).

questions.subject: Physics
questions.text: The value of g decreases as one moves from the Earth's surface towards its centre mainly because
options: only the mass of Earth enclosed within that radius contributes to the gravitational pull
the Earth's rotation increases with depth
questions.explanation: Inside a uniform sphere, only the mass enclosed within the radius from the centre contributes net gravitational force, so g decreases towards the centre, reaching zero there.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.text: Escape velocity is defined as the minimum velocity needed for an object to
options: achieve a stable circular orbit close to the surface
orbit a planet at a constant altitude
completely escape a planet's gravitational field without further propulsion
questions.explanation: Escape velocity is the speed at which an object's kinetic energy equals the gravitational potential energy binding it, allowing it to escape to infinity.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.text: The weight of an object is best described as
options: the gravitational force acting on its mass
the amount of matter it contains
the same everywhere in the universe
a measure independent of gravitational field strength
questions.explanation: Weight (W = mg) is a force resulting from the gravitational pull on an object's mass, and therefore varies with the local gravitational field strength, unlike mass.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.text: A satellite in a stable circular orbit around the Earth experiences a centripetal force provided by
options: the Earth's gravitational attraction on the satellite
questions.explanation: For a satellite in circular orbit, gravity supplies exactly the centripetal force needed to keep it moving in its circular path around the Earth.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.text: The centre of gravity of an object is the point at which
options: the object's mass is exactly zero
all external forces cancel to zero
the entire weight of the object may be considered to act
questions.explanation: The centre of gravity is the single point through which the resultant of all gravitational forces on the parts of a body can be considered to act.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.text: An object is in stable equilibrium if, when slightly displaced, it
options: remains in its new position permanently
moves further away from its original position
questions.explanation: Stable equilibrium is characterised by a restoring tendency: a small displacement raises the centre of gravity, and gravity pulls the object back to its lowest-energy position.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.text: A body with a low centre of gravity and a wide base is generally
options: more stable than one with a high centre of gravity and narrow base
unaffected by the position of its centre of gravity
less stable than a tall, narrow object
questions.explanation: A wide base and low centre of gravity require a greater tilt before the centre of gravity passes outside the base, making the object harder to topple, hence more stable.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.text: The Principle of Moments states that for a body in equilibrium under the action of several coplanar forces,
options: the sum of clockwise moments about any point equals the sum of anticlockwise moments about that point
moments are only considered for forces acting at the centre of gravity
all forces must be equal in magnitude
the net force must be greater than zero
questions.explanation: The Principle of Moments (law of the lever) requires that clockwise and anticlockwise turning effects about a pivot balance exactly for rotational equilibrium.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.text: A uniform metre rule is balanced at its 50 cm mark. A 2 N weight is hung at the 20 cm mark. Where must a 4 N weight be hung to balance it?
questions.explanation: Clockwise moment of 4 N about 50 cm mark = anticlockwise moment of 2 N: 2 x 30 = 4 x d, so d = 15 cm from the pivot, placing it at 50 + 15 = 65 cm.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.text: Lami's Theorem applies to three coplanar, concurrent forces in equilibrium and states that each force is proportional to the
options: sine of the angle between the other two forces
cosine of the angle between the other two forces
sum of the other two forces
tangent of the angle between the other two forces
questions.explanation: Lami's Theorem: F1/sin(angle between F2,F3) = F2/sin(angle between F1,F3) = F3/sin(angle between F1,F2), useful for solving three-force equilibrium problems.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.text: Work done by a force is calculated as the product of the
options: force and the distance moved in the direction of the force
questions.explanation: Work (W = Fd cos theta) is done when a force causes displacement in its own direction; no work is done if there is no displacement or the force is perpendicular to it.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.text: A force of 10 N moves an object through a distance of 5 m in the direction of the force. How much work is done?
questions.explanation: Work = Force x distance = 10 x 5 = 50 joules.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.text: Kinetic energy of a moving body is given by the formula
questions.explanation: Kinetic energy, the energy of motion, is given by KE = 1/2 mv^2, where m is mass and v is velocity.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.text: A 2 kg object falls freely and reaches a velocity of 10 m/s. What is its kinetic energy at that instant?

questions.subject: Physics
questions.text: Gravitational potential energy is given by the formula
questions.explanation: Gravitational potential energy depends on mass (m), the acceleration due to gravity (g), and height (h) above a reference level: PE = mgh.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.text: The Law of Conservation of Energy states that
options: kinetic energy is always equal to potential energy
energy cannot be created or destroyed, only transformed from one form to another
total energy of a system always increases over time
energy is always lost as heat in any process
questions.explanation: This fundamental physical law means the total energy in an isolated system remains constant, even as it changes form (e.g., potential to kinetic).

questions.subject: Physics
questions.text: Power is defined as the
options: rate at which work is done
questions.explanation: Power (P = W/t) measures how quickly work is performed or energy is transferred, measured in watts (joules per second).

questions.subject: Physics
questions.text: A machine does 500 J of work in 10 seconds. What is its power output?
questions.explanation: Power = Work/time = 500/10 = 50 watts.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.text: Friction is a force that always acts to
options: increase the speed of a moving object
oppose relative motion or the tendency of motion between two surfaces
act perpendicular to the surfaces in contact
questions.explanation: Friction is a resistive force arising from contact between surfaces, always acting opposite to the direction of relative motion or intended motion.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.text: Static friction differs from dynamic (kinetic) friction in that static friction
options: does not depend on the normal force
is always smaller than dynamic friction
acts on objects that are not yet moving relative to each other
questions.explanation: Static friction prevents relative motion from starting, and its maximum value is generally slightly greater than the kinetic (dynamic) friction that acts once motion begins.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.text: Viscosity refers to a fluid's internal resistance to
questions.explanation: Viscosity measures how strongly a fluid resists flowing or deforming; thick fluids like honey have high viscosity compared to water.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.text: Terminal velocity is reached by an object falling through a fluid when
options: the resistive (drag) force equals the object's weight, resulting in zero net acceleration
questions.explanation: As speed increases, drag force increases until it balances gravity; at this point the object falls at a constant maximum speed, its terminal velocity.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.text: The mechanical advantage of a simple machine is defined as the ratio of
options: distance moved by effort to distance moved by load
questions.explanation: Mechanical advantage (MA) = load/effort, indicating how many times the machine multiplies the applied effort force.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.text: The velocity ratio of a simple machine is defined as the ratio of
options: distance moved by the effort to distance moved by the load
questions.explanation: Velocity ratio (VR) = distance moved by effort / distance moved by load, a purely geometric property of the machine, independent of friction.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.text: The efficiency of a machine is calculated as
questions.explanation: Efficiency = (MA/VR) x 100%, reflecting how much of the input work is usefully converted to output work, always less than 100% due to friction.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.text: A pulley system has a velocity ratio of 4 and requires an effort of 30 N to lift a load of 100 N. What is its efficiency?
questions.explanation: MA = load/effort = 100/30 = 3.33. Efficiency = (MA/VR) x 100 = (3.33/4) x 100 = about 83.3%.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.text: Hooke's Law states that within the elastic limit, the extension of a spring is
options: inversely proportional to the applied force
proportional to the square of the applied force
directly proportional to the applied force
questions.explanation: Hooke's Law: F = ke, where extension e is directly proportional to the applied force F, provided the elastic limit of the material is not exceeded.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.text: Young's modulus of a material is defined as the ratio of
options: stress to strain, within the elastic limit
questions.explanation: Young's modulus (E = stress/strain) quantifies a material's stiffness, describing how much it deforms elastically under a given stress.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.text: Atmospheric pressure is caused mainly by
options: the weight of the column of air above a given point
temperature differences at ground level only
the presence of water vapour alone
questions.explanation: The atmosphere's weight, pressing down due to gravity, exerts a pressure on surfaces below it, which decreases with increasing altitude.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.text: Pascal's Principle states that pressure applied to an enclosed fluid is
options: reduced as it moves through the fluid
transmitted equally in all directions throughout the fluid
only transmitted in the direction of the applied force
questions.explanation: Pascal's Principle underlies hydraulic systems: pressure applied anywhere in a confined incompressible fluid is transmitted undiminished to all parts of the fluid.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.text: Archimedes' Principle states that the upthrust on a body partially or wholly immersed in a fluid equals the
options: weight of the fluid displaced by the body
questions.explanation: Archimedes' Principle explains buoyancy: the upward force (upthrust) on a submerged object equals the weight of the fluid it displaces.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.text: The pressure exerted by a liquid column depends on the
options: surface area of the container base only
depth of the liquid, its density, and the acceleration due to gravity
questions.explanation: Liquid pressure is given by P = h(rho)g, depending on the height (depth) of the column, the liquid's density, and gravitational acceleration, but not on the container's shape.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.text: A body floats in a liquid when
options: there is no upthrust acting on it
the upthrust exceeds twice its weight
its density is greater than that of the liquid
the upthrust on it equals its weight
questions.explanation: For a floating object, the upward buoyant force (upthrust) exactly balances the downward weight, resulting in zero net force and equilibrium.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.text: A spring of natural length 20 cm extends to 25 cm under a load of 10 N. What is its spring constant?
questions.explanation: Extension e = 25 - 20 = 5 cm. Spring constant k = F/e = 10/5 = 2 N/cm.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.text: The Celsius and Kelvin temperature scales are related by the formula
questions.explanation: To convert Celsius to Kelvin (the absolute temperature scale), add 273 (more precisely 273.15) to the Celsius value.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.text: When a solid is heated, it generally expands because
options: the mass of the solid decreases
increased thermal energy causes particles to vibrate more and move slightly further apart
questions.explanation: Thermal expansion occurs because heating increases the amplitude of particle vibrations, increasing the average spacing between them.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.text: According to Boyle's Law, at constant temperature, the pressure of a fixed mass of gas is
questions.explanation: Boyle's Law: PV = constant at constant temperature, so pressure increases as volume decreases, and vice versa.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.text: According to Charles's Law, at constant pressure, the volume of a fixed mass of gas is
options: inversely proportional to its absolute temperature
directly proportional to its absolute temperature
questions.explanation: Charles's Law: V/T = constant at constant pressure, meaning gas volume increases proportionally with absolute (Kelvin) temperature.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.text: The Pressure Law states that at constant volume, the pressure of a fixed mass of gas is
options: inversely proportional to its absolute temperature
directly proportional to its absolute temperature
questions.explanation: The Pressure (Gay-Lussac's) Law: P/T = constant at constant volume, so pressure rises proportionally with absolute temperature.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.text: Specific heat capacity of a substance is defined as the quantity of heat required to raise the temperature of
options: the whole substance by any amount
a unit volume of the substance by ten degrees
one mole of the substance to its boiling point
a unit mass of the substance by one degree (Celsius or Kelvin)
questions.explanation: Specific heat capacity, c, is defined by Q = mcT-change, representing heat needed per unit mass per degree temperature rise.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.text: How much heat is needed to raise the temperature of 2 kg of water by 5 degC? (Specific heat capacity of water = 4200 J/kgK)
questions.explanation: Q = mcT-change = 2 x 4200 x 5 = 42000 J.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.text: Latent heat of fusion is the heat energy required to
options: cool a liquid to its freezing point
raise the temperature of a solid by one degree
change a substance from liquid to gas
change a substance from solid to liquid at constant temperature
questions.explanation: Latent heat of fusion is absorbed during melting (solid to liquid) without any change in temperature, as the energy breaks intermolecular bonds rather than increasing kinetic energy.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.text: Heat transfer through a solid medium, without the bulk movement of the material itself, is called
questions.explanation: Conduction transfers heat through direct particle-to-particle vibration and collision within a solid, without any overall movement of the medium.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.text: Convection as a mode of heat transfer occurs mainly in
options: liquids and gases, through the bulk movement of the fluid
questions.explanation: Convection relies on the physical movement of heated fluid (liquid or gas), which is less dense and rises, carrying thermal energy with it, a process not possible in rigid solids.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.text: The distance between two successive crests (or troughs) of a wave is called its
questions.explanation: Wavelength (usually denoted by the Greek letter lambda) is the spatial period of a wave, the distance over which the wave's shape repeats.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.text: The relationship between the velocity, frequency, and wavelength of a wave is given by
questions.explanation: The wave equation v = f(lambda) relates wave speed to the product of frequency and wavelength, valid for all types of waves.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.text: Sound waves are classified as
questions.explanation: In sound waves, particles of the medium vibrate parallel to the direction of wave propagation, characteristic of longitudinal waves, unlike transverse waves such as light.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.text: An echo is produced when sound waves
options: are refracted through a different medium
are absorbed completely by a surface
are reflected off a hard surface and return to the listener after a short delay
questions.explanation: Echoes result from sound reflecting off obstacles like walls or cliffs, reaching the listener again after enough delay to be perceived as a distinct repetition.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.text: Sound cannot travel through a vacuum because
options: sound waves travel faster in a vacuum
it requires a material medium (solid, liquid, or gas) for particle-to-particle transmission
sound waves are electromagnetic in nature
questions.explanation: Unlike electromagnetic waves such as light, sound is a mechanical wave that needs particles of a medium to vibrate and transmit the disturbance.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.text: The pitch of a musical note is determined mainly by its
questions.explanation: Higher frequency sound waves are perceived as higher pitch, while amplitude instead determines the loudness of the sound.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.text: The loudness of a sound is determined mainly by its
questions.explanation: A sound wave with greater amplitude carries more energy, which is perceived by the ear as a louder sound.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.text: The Doppler effect explains why the pitch of a sound
options: appears to change when there is relative motion between the source and the observer
depends only on the medium's temperature
cannot be perceived by the human ear
is always constant regardless of motion
questions.explanation: The Doppler effect describes the apparent shift in frequency (and pitch) of a wave due to relative motion, e.g., a siren sounding higher-pitched as it approaches and lower as it recedes.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.text: The law of reflection states that the angle of incidence is
options: unrelated to the angle of reflection
equal to the angle of reflection
always greater than the angle of reflection
questions.explanation: The law of reflection states that the angle between the incident ray and the normal equals the angle between the reflected ray and the normal.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.text: Refraction of light occurs when light
options: travels through a vacuum without any medium
reflects off a mirror at equal angles
passes from one medium to another of different optical density, causing a change in speed and direction
is completely absorbed by a surface
questions.explanation: Refraction is the bending of light as it crosses a boundary between media with different refractive indices, due to a change in wave speed.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.text: A concave mirror is also known as a
questions.explanation: Concave mirrors curve inward and reflect parallel rays to converge at a focal point, making them converging mirrors, used in torches and telescopes.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.text: A convex lens forms a real, inverted image when the object is placed
options: beyond the focal length of the lens
between the lens and its focal point
exactly at the optical centre of the lens
at infinity, producing an image at the focal point only
questions.explanation: When an object is placed beyond the focal length of a convex lens, the lens converges the refracted rays to form a real, inverted image on the other side.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.text: A ray of white light passing through a glass prism separates into its component colours, a phenomenon known as
questions.explanation: Dispersion occurs because different wavelengths (colours) of light are refracted by slightly different amounts, spreading white light into a spectrum.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.text: The image formed by a plane mirror is always
options: virtual, upright, and the same size as the object
questions.explanation: A plane mirror always produces a virtual (cannot be projected on a screen), laterally inverted, upright image identical in size to the object.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.text: A simple microscope works on the principle of using a
options: prism to disperse light into colours
single converging lens to produce a magnified, virtual image of a nearby object
plane mirror to reflect an image
concave mirror to focus distant objects
questions.explanation: A simple microscope (magnifying glass) uses one convex lens, with the object placed within its focal length to produce an enlarged, upright, virtual image.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.text: A refracting astronomical telescope typically uses
options: two converging lenses: an objective lens and an eyepiece lens
one convex lens and one plane mirror
questions.explanation: A basic refracting telescope has an objective lens that forms a real image of a distant object, magnified further by the eyepiece lens acting as a simple magnifier.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.text: Electrostatics is the study of
options: the flow of heat through conductors
questions.explanation: Electrostatics deals with stationary electric charges and the forces, fields, and potentials associated with them, as opposed to current electricity.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.text: Like electric charges (e.g., two positive charges) placed near each other will
options: have no effect on each other
questions.explanation: Coulomb's Law describes how like charges repel while unlike charges attract, a fundamental behaviour of electrostatic forces.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.text: A capacitor is a device used mainly to
options: store electric charge (and energy) in an electric field
generate electric current from mechanical motion
questions.explanation: A capacitor consists of two conducting plates separated by an insulator (dielectric), storing charge and energy when a potential difference is applied across it.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.text: Ohm's Law states that the current flowing through a conductor is directly proportional to the potential difference across it, provided that
options: temperature and other physical conditions remain constant
questions.explanation: Ohm's Law (V = IR) holds for ohmic conductors as long as physical conditions such as temperature remain unchanged during the measurement.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.text: A current of 2 A flows through a resistor of resistance 5 ohms. What is the potential difference across the resistor?
questions.explanation: Using V = IR: V = 2 x 5 = 10 volts.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.text: When resistors are connected in series, the total resistance is
options: equal to the average of the individual resistances
the sum of the individual resistances
always less than the smallest individual resistance
the reciprocal of the sum of reciprocals of individual resistances
questions.explanation: In a series circuit, resistances simply add: Rtotal = R1 + R2 + R3 + ..., since the same current flows through each resistor in turn.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.text: When resistors are connected in parallel, the reciprocal of the total resistance equals the
options: sum of the reciprocals of the individual resistances
questions.explanation: For parallel resistors: 1/Rtotal = 1/R1 + 1/R2 + ..., which always gives a total resistance smaller than the smallest individual resistor.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.text: A magnetic field is produced around a straight, current-carrying conductor in a pattern of
options: straight lines parallel to the wire
a uniform field identical to a bar magnet
no field at all unless the current is very large
questions.explanation: Oersted's discovery showed that a current-carrying wire produces a magnetic field forming concentric circles around it, with direction given by the right-hand grip rule.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.text: Electromagnetic induction is the process by which
options: current flows through a conductor at absolute zero with no resistance
a magnet is created by passing current through a coil
a changing magnetic field induces an electromotive force (e.m.f.) in a nearby conductor
static charges build up on an insulator
questions.explanation: Faraday's Law of electromagnetic induction states that a changing magnetic flux through a circuit induces an e.m.f., the basis for generators and transformers.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.text: A transformer works on the principle of
options: mutual electromagnetic induction between two coils linked by a changing magnetic flux
questions.explanation: Transformers use a changing current in a primary coil to produce a varying magnetic flux, which induces a corresponding e.m.f. in a secondary coil, enabling voltage step-up or step-down.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.text: In Bohr's model of the atom, electrons orbit the nucleus in
options: a single fixed orbit for all elements
orbits that constantly radiate energy and spiral inward
fixed, discrete energy levels (orbits) without radiating energy
continuously variable orbits at any energy
questions.explanation: Bohr proposed that electrons occupy specific quantised energy levels, and only emit or absorb energy when jumping between these fixed levels, not while orbiting.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.text: The photoelectric effect refers to the
options: reflection of light off a polished metal surface
emission of light when a metal is heated
emission of electrons from a metal surface when light of sufficient frequency shines on it
absorption of electrons by a metal surface in the dark
questions.explanation: The photoelectric effect occurs when incident photons with energy above a metal's threshold frequency eject electrons from its surface, evidence for the particle nature of light.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.text: X-rays are a form of
options: charged particles emitted from radioactive nuclei
sound waves of very high pitch
questions.explanation: X-rays are electromagnetic waves with very short wavelength and high frequency, produced when fast-moving electrons are suddenly decelerated, as in an X-ray tube.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.text: Radioactivity is the spontaneous process by which
options: unstable atomic nuclei emit particles or radiation to become more stable
atoms absorb external radiation to become excited
molecules break apart due to heating alone
electrons are shared between two atoms
questions.explanation: Radioactive decay occurs when an unstable nucleus spontaneously emits alpha, beta, or gamma radiation, transforming into a more stable configuration.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.text: In the equation F = kv², where F is force in newtons and v is velocity in m/s, what is the SI unit of the constant k?
questions.explanation: k = F/v² = (kg m s⁻²)/(m² s⁻²) = kg/m, so k must carry units of kilograms per metre.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.text: What is the dimension of impulse (the product of force and time)?
questions.explanation: Impulse equals change in momentum, so its dimension is the same as momentum: mass x velocity = M x LT⁻¹ = MLT⁻¹.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.text: For a simple pendulum, T = 2π√(l/g), where l is length and g is acceleration due to gravity. What is the dimension of √(l/g)?
questions.explanation: l/g has dimension L/(LT⁻²) = T², so its square root has dimension T, consistent with T being a time period.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.text: A ball is projected horizontally from the top of a cliff 45 m high with a speed of 20 m/s. Taking g = 10 m/s², how long does it take to hit the ground?
questions.explanation: Vertical motion only: h = ½gt², so 45 = ½(10)t², t² = 9, t = 3 s (horizontal speed does not affect fall time).

questions.subject: Physics
questions.text: A ball is projected horizontally from a cliff top with a speed of 20 m/s and takes 3 s to land. What horizontal distance (range) does it travel?
questions.explanation: Horizontal velocity is constant during projectile motion, so range = v x t = 20 x 3 = 60 m.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.text: A projectile is launched at 30° to the horizontal with an initial speed of 40 m/s. Taking g = 10 m/s², calculate the maximum height reached.
questions.explanation: Vertical component u_y = 40 sin30° = 20 m/s. Maximum height H = u_y²/(2g) = 400/20 = 20 m.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.text: A projectile is launched at 30° to the horizontal with an initial speed of 40 m/s. Taking g = 10 m/s², calculate its total time of flight.
questions.explanation: u_y = 40 sin30° = 20 m/s. Time of flight T = 2u_y/g = 2(20)/10 = 4 s.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.text: Two masses, 3 kg and 5 kg, are connected by a light inextensible string over a frictionless pulley. Taking g = 10 m/s², calculate the acceleration of the system.
questions.explanation: For an Atwood machine, a = (m2 - m1)g/(m1 + m2) = (5 - 3)(10)/(3 + 5) = 20/8 = 2.5 m/s².

questions.subject: Physics
questions.text: In an Atwood machine with masses 3 kg and 5 kg over a frictionless pulley (g = 10 m/s², acceleration = 2.5 m/s²), calculate the tension in the string.
questions.explanation: Using the lighter mass: T - m1g = m1a, so T = m1(g + a) = 3(10 + 2.5) = 37.5 N (also equals m2(g - a) = 5(7.5) = 37.5 N, confirming consistency).

questions.subject: Physics
questions.text: A car of mass 1000 kg moves round a circular track of radius 50 m at a constant speed of 20 m/s. Calculate the centripetal force required.
questions.explanation: Centripetal force F = mv²/r = 1000(20²)/50 = 1000(400)/50 = 8000 N.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.text: A 4 kg trolley moving at 6 m/s collides with a stationary 2 kg trolley and sticks to it. Calculate their common velocity just after collision.
questions.explanation: By conservation of momentum: m1u1 = (m1+m2)v, so v = (4 x 6)/(4+2) = 24/6 = 4 m/s.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.text: A 10 kg block rests on a horizontal surface where the coefficient of friction between the block and surface is 0.4. Taking g = 10 m/s², what minimum horizontal force is needed to just start the block moving?
questions.explanation: The limiting frictional force is F = μmg = 0.4 x 10 x 10 = 40 N, the minimum applied force needed to overcome static friction.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.text: A car decelerates uniformly from 30 m/s to rest in 6 s. Calculate the distance it covers before stopping.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.text: A crane lifts a load of 500 kg through a height of 10 m in 25 s. Taking g = 10 m/s², calculate the power developed by the crane.
questions.explanation: Work done = mgh = 500 x 10 x 10 = 50000 J. Power = W/t = 50000/25 = 2000 W.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.text: An inclined plane 5 m long rises to a height of 1 m. A force of 100 N pushes a load of 400 N up the incline at constant speed. Calculate the efficiency of the incline.
questions.explanation: Velocity ratio = length/height = 5/1 = 5. Mechanical advantage = load/effort = 400/100 = 4. Efficiency = (MA/VR) x 100 = (4/5) x 100 = 80%.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.text: A ball of mass 0.5 kg is dropped from a height of 20 m. Taking g = 10 m/s² and neglecting air resistance, calculate its velocity just before hitting the ground.
questions.explanation: Using v² = 2gh: v² = 2(10)(20) = 400, so v = 20 m/s.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.text: A 0.5 kg ball is dropped from a height of 20 m (g = 10 m/s², air resistance negligible). Calculate its kinetic energy after it has fallen 10 m.
questions.explanation: Total mechanical energy = mgh = 0.5 x 10 x 20 = 100 J. At the halfway point, PE lost = mg(10) = 50 J, so KE gained = 50 J.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.text: A pulley system has a velocity ratio of 3. An effort of 300 N raises a load of 600 N. Calculate the efficiency of the system.
questions.explanation: Mechanical advantage = load/effort = 600/300 = 2. Efficiency = (MA/VR) x 100 = (2/3) x 100 = 66.7%.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.text: A 2000 kg car moving at 15 m/s is brought to rest over a distance of 50 m by a constant braking force. Calculate the magnitude of the braking force.
questions.explanation: KE lost = ½mv² = ½(2000)(15²) = 225000 J. Since this work is done by the braking force over 50 m, F = 225000/50 = 4500 N.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.text: A pump raises 200 kg of water through a height of 15 m every 10 seconds. Taking g = 10 m/s², calculate the power of the pump.
questions.explanation: Work done per cycle = mgh = 200 x 10 x 15 = 30000 J in 10 s, so power = 30000/10 = 3000 W.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.text: A uniform, weightless lever of length 2 m is used to lift a load of 300 N placed 0.4 m from the pivot, with effort applied 1.6 m from the pivot on the other side. Calculate the effort required.
questions.explanation: By the principle of moments: load x load-arm = effort x effort-arm, so 300 x 0.4 = effort x 1.6, giving effort = 120/1.6 = 75 N.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.text: A machine has a velocity ratio of 5 and an efficiency of 80%. Calculate the effort required to lift a load of 1000 N using this machine.
questions.explanation: Efficiency = (MA/VR) x 100, so MA = 0.8 x 5 = 4. Effort = load/MA = 1000/4 = 250 N.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.text: A cyclist free-wheels down a hill of height 45 m with negligible energy losses. Taking g = 10 m/s², calculate the speed gained.
questions.explanation: By energy conservation, v² = 2gh = 2(10)(45) = 900, so v = 30 m/s.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.text: A wire of original length 2 m and cross-sectional area 1 x 10⁻⁶ m² extends by 1 mm under a load of 100 N. Calculate the Young's modulus of the wire material.
questions.explanation: Stress = F/A = 100/(1x10⁻⁶) = 1x10⁸ Pa. Strain = e/L = 0.001/2 = 5x10⁻⁴. Young's modulus = stress/strain = 1x10⁸/5x10⁻⁴ = 2x10¹¹ Pa.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.text: A spring with force constant 200 N/m is stretched by 0.1 m. Calculate the elastic potential energy stored in the spring.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.text: A uniform plank of length 6 m and weight 120 N is pivoted at its centre. A boy weighing 300 N stands 1 m from the pivot on one side. How far from the pivot must a 200 N girl stand on the other side to balance the plank?
questions.explanation: Since the plank is uniform and pivoted at its centre, its own weight produces no net moment. Balancing moments: 300 x 1 = 200 x d, so d = 300/200 = 1.5 m.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.text: Three coplanar forces act at a point in equilibrium: Q = 30 N and R = 40 N act at right angles to each other, and a third force P balances them. Calculate the magnitude of P.
questions.explanation: For equilibrium, P must be equal in magnitude and opposite in direction to the resultant of Q and R: resultant = √(30²+40²) = √2500 = 50 N, so P = 50 N.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.text: A wire of diameter 2 mm is subjected to a stretching force of 157 N. Calculate the stress in the wire.
questions.explanation: Radius = 1 mm = 1x10⁻³ m, so area = πr² = π(1x10⁻³)² ≈ 3.14x10⁻⁶ m². Stress = F/A = 157/3.14x10⁻⁶ ≈ 5x10⁷ Pa.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.text: A uniform ladder of length 5 m leans against a smooth vertical wall with its foot 3 m from the base of the wall on rough ground. Calculate the angle the ladder makes with the ground.
questions.explanation: The ladder, wall, and ground form a 3-4-5 right triangle. The angle with the ground has adjacent = 3 m and hypotenuse = 5 m, so cosθ = 3/5, giving θ = 53.1°.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.text: A solid weighs 5 N in air and 3 N when fully submerged in water. Calculate the upthrust on the solid.
questions.explanation: Upthrust = apparent loss of weight = weight in air - weight in water = 5 - 3 = 2 N.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.text: A solid weighs 5 N in air and 3 N when fully submerged in water. Calculate the relative density of the solid.
questions.explanation: Relative density = weight in air / upthrust = 5 / (5-3) = 5/2 = 2.5.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.text: Calculate the pressure at a depth of 10 m in water (density = 1000 kg/m³, g = 10 m/s²), ignoring atmospheric pressure.
questions.explanation: Liquid pressure P = hρg = 10 x 1000 x 10 = 100000 Pa = 1 x 10⁵ Pa.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.text: A diver is 10 m below the surface of water (density 1000 kg/m³, g = 10 m/s²). If atmospheric pressure is 1.0 x 10⁵ Pa, calculate the total pressure experienced by the diver.
questions.explanation: Total pressure = atmospheric pressure + liquid pressure = 1x10⁵ + (10x1000x10) = 1x10⁵ + 1x10⁵ = 2x10⁵ Pa.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.text: A block of wood of density 0.6 g/cm³ and volume 200 cm³ floats in water of density 1.0 g/cm³. Calculate the volume of the block submerged.
questions.explanation: For floating, weight = upthrust, so fraction submerged = density of object/density of liquid = 0.6/1.0 = 0.6. Volume submerged = 0.6 x 200 = 120 cm³.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.text: In a hydraulic press, the small piston has an area of 5 cm² and the large piston has an area of 100 cm². If a force of 20 N is applied to the small piston, calculate the force exerted on the large piston.
questions.explanation: By Pascal's Principle, pressure is transmitted equally: F1/A1 = F2/A2, so F2 = F1(A2/A1) = 20(100/5) = 400 N.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.text: A mercury thermometer has its ice point mark at 2 cm and its steam point mark at 22 cm on the stem. What temperature is indicated by a mercury level at 8 cm?
questions.explanation: Temperature = [(length - ice point)/(steam point - ice point)] x 100 = [(8-2)/(22-2)] x 100 = (6/20) x 100 = 30°C.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.text: A gas has a volume of 300 cm³ at 27°C. Calculate its volume at 127°C if the pressure is kept constant.
questions.explanation: By Charles's Law, V1/T1 = V2/T2 (in kelvin): 300/300 = V2/400, so V2 = 300 x 400/300 = 400 cm³.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.text: A gas occupies 500 cm³ at a pressure of 2 x 10⁵ Pa. Calculate its volume when the pressure increases to 5 x 10⁵ Pa at constant temperature.
questions.explanation: By Boyle's Law, P1V1 = P2V2: V2 = (2x10⁵ x 500)/(5x10⁵) = 200 cm³.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.text: A fixed mass of gas at 27°C has a pressure of 1.0 x 10⁵ Pa in a sealed rigid container. Calculate the pressure when the temperature rises to 127°C.
questions.explanation: By the Pressure Law, P1/T1 = P2/T2 (kelvin): P2 = P1(T2/T1) = 1x10⁵ x (400/300) = 1.33 x 10⁵ Pa.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.text: A gas at pressure 1 x 10⁵ Pa, volume 400 cm³, and temperature 300 K is changed to a pressure of 2 x 10⁵ Pa and temperature 600 K. Calculate the new volume.
questions.explanation: Using the combined gas law P1V1/T1 = P2V2/T2: V2 = (P1V1T2)/(T1P2) = (1x10⁵ x 400 x 600)/(300 x 2x10⁵) = 400 cm³.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.text: A perfect black body is best described as a body that
options: absorbs all radiation incident on it and, for its temperature, emits the maximum possible radiation
reflects all radiation incident on it
transmits all radiation incident on it without absorption
absorbs only visible light and reflects the rest
questions.explanation: A perfect black body is a theoretical ideal absorber and emitter of thermal radiation, absorbing all incident radiation and radiating the maximum possible amount for its temperature.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.text: A metal rod of length 2 m and cross-sectional area 0.01 m² has its ends kept at 100°C and 20°C. If the thermal conductivity of the metal is 400 W/mK, calculate the rate of heat conduction through the rod.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.text: Convection currents are set up in a room heated by a radiator mainly because
options: warm air near the radiator becomes less dense and rises, being replaced by cooler, denser air
cold air sinks and heats up purely by compression
heat travels in straight lines from the radiator without needing a medium
warm air near the radiator becomes denser and sinks to the floor
questions.explanation: Convection relies on density differences: air heated by the radiator expands, becomes less dense, and rises, while cooler denser air flows in to replace it, setting up a circulating current.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.text: A black surface and a white surface at the same temperature are placed in sunlight. The black surface becomes hotter mainly because black surfaces are
options: better conductors of heat than white surfaces
better reflectors of radiation than white surfaces
better absorbers (and emitters) of radiant heat than white or shiny surfaces
surfaces with a lower specific heat capacity than white surfaces
questions.explanation: Dull black surfaces absorb (and emit) thermal radiation much more effectively than white or shiny surfaces, which reflect more radiation, so the black surface heats up faster.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.text: Calculate the quantity of heat required to convert 0.5 kg of water at 100°C completely into steam at 100°C, given the specific latent heat of vaporization of water is 2.26 x 10⁶ J/kg.
questions.explanation: Heat required Q = mL = 0.5 x 2.26x10⁶ = 1.13 x 10⁶ J.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.text: Calculate the total heat required to convert 2 kg of ice at 0°C completely to water at 0°C, given the specific latent heat of fusion of ice is 3.36 x 10⁵ J/kg.
questions.explanation: Heat required Q = mL = 2 x 3.36x10⁵ = 6.72 x 10⁵ J.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.text: 200 g of water at 80°C is mixed with 300 g of water at 20°C. Assuming no heat is lost, calculate the final temperature of the mixture.
questions.explanation: Heat lost by hot water = heat gained by cold water: 200(80-Tf) = 300(Tf-20). Solving: 16000-200Tf = 300Tf-6000, so 22000 = 500Tf, Tf = 44°C.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.text: A 0.1 kg piece of metal at 100°C is dropped into 0.2 kg of water at 20°C in a calorimeter of negligible heat capacity. If the final temperature is 25°C, calculate the specific heat capacity of the metal (specific heat capacity of water = 4200 J/kgK).
questions.explanation: Heat lost by metal = heat gained by water: 0.1 x c x (100-25) = 0.2 x 4200 x (25-20). So 7.5c = 4200, c = 4200/7.5 = 560 J/kgK.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.text: Evaporation differs from boiling mainly in that evaporation
options: occurs at any temperature and only at the surface of the liquid, unlike boiling which occurs at a fixed temperature throughout the liquid
occurs only at the boiling point, throughout the liquid
requires no input of energy whatsoever
can only occur inside a sealed vacuum flask
questions.explanation: Evaporation is a surface phenomenon that can occur at any temperature, while boiling occurs throughout the bulk of the liquid only at its fixed boiling point.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.text: Calculate the total heat needed to convert 1 kg of ice at -10°C to water at 0°C, given specific heat capacity of ice = 2100 J/kgK and specific latent heat of fusion of ice = 336000 J/kg.
questions.explanation: Heat to warm ice to 0°C: Q1 = mcΔT = 1x2100x10 = 21000 J. Heat to melt ice: Q2 = mL = 1x336000 = 336000 J. Total = 21000+336000 = 357000 J = 3.57x10⁵ J.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.text: A wave has a frequency of 500 Hz and a wavelength of 0.68 m. Calculate its speed.
questions.explanation: Wave speed v = fλ = 500 x 0.68 = 340 m/s.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.text: Radio waves travel at the speed of light, 3 x 10⁸ m/s. Calculate the wavelength of a radio wave of frequency 1 x 10⁶ Hz (1 MHz).

questions.subject: Physics
questions.text: A string of length 0.5 m, vibrating in its fundamental mode, produces a note of frequency 320 Hz. Calculate the speed of the wave on the string.
questions.explanation: In the fundamental mode, the string length equals half a wavelength, so λ = 2L = 1.0 m. Speed v = fλ = 320 x 1.0 = 320 m/s.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.text: A wave has a period of 0.02 s. Calculate its frequency.
questions.explanation: Frequency f = 1/T = 1/0.02 = 50 Hz.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.text: Two coherent sources produce waves of wavelength 4 cm. Calculate the minimum path difference required for destructive interference.
questions.explanation: Destructive interference first occurs when the path difference equals half a wavelength: λ/2 = 4/2 = 2 cm.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.text: An object is placed 30 cm from a concave mirror of focal length 10 cm. Calculate the image distance.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.text: An object is placed 30 cm from a concave mirror, forming an image 15 cm from the mirror. Calculate the linear magnification of the image.
questions.explanation: Magnification m = v/u = 15/30 = 0.5, indicating the image is diminished compared to the object.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.text: An object is placed 20 cm in front of a convex mirror of focal length 15 cm (f = -15 cm by convention). Describe the image formed.
options: real, inverted, and located about 8.6 cm in front of the mirror
virtual and located 60 cm behind the mirror
real and located 20 cm in front of the mirror
virtual, upright, and located about 8.6 cm behind the mirror
questions.explanation: 1/v = 1/f - 1/u = -1/15 - 1/20 = -7/60, so v ≈ -8.57 cm. The negative sign shows the image is virtual, upright, and behind the mirror.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.text: Two plane mirrors are inclined at 60° to each other. Calculate the number of images formed of an object placed between them.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.text: An object is placed at a distance equal to twice the focal length (2f) from a concave mirror. What describes the image formed?
options: virtual, upright, and magnified, on the same side as the object
real, inverted, the same size as the object, and located at 2f
real, inverted, magnified, and located beyond 2f
virtual, diminished, and located between the mirror and the focus
questions.explanation: When an object is placed at the centre of curvature (2f) of a concave mirror, the image formed is real, inverted, the same size as the object, and also located at 2f.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.text: A ray of light passes from air into glass of refractive index 1.5 at an angle of incidence of 30°. Calculate the angle of refraction.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.text: Calculate the critical angle for a glass-air boundary if the refractive index of the glass is 1.5.
questions.explanation: Critical angle C satisfies sinC = 1/n = 1/1.5 = 0.667, so C = sin⁻¹(0.667) ≈ 41.8°.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.text: A coin at the bottom of a beaker of water (real depth 20 cm) appears to be at a depth of 15 cm when viewed from directly above. Calculate the refractive index of the water.
questions.explanation: Refractive index = real depth/apparent depth = 20/15 = 1.33.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.text: An object is placed 15 cm from a converging lens of focal length 10 cm. Calculate the image distance.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.text: An object placed 15 cm from a converging lens of focal length 10 cm forms an image 30 cm from the lens. Calculate the linear magnification.
questions.explanation: Magnification m = v/u = 30/15 = 2, so the image is twice the size of the object.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.text: Calculate the power of a converging lens of focal length 25 cm.
questions.explanation: Power P = 1/f, with f in metres: f = 0.25 m, so P = 1/0.25 = 4 dioptres.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.text: Total internal reflection occurs at a boundary between a denser and a less dense medium when the angle of incidence in the denser medium
options: exceeds the critical angle for that pair of media
is less than the critical angle for that pair of media
occurs only when light travels from a less dense to a denser medium
questions.explanation: Total internal reflection happens only when light travels from a denser to a less dense medium and the angle of incidence exceeds the critical angle, so no light is transmitted.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.text: An object is placed 20 cm from a diverging (concave) lens of focal length 10 cm (f = -10 cm by convention). Describe the image formed.
options: real and located 6.67 cm on the opposite side of the lens
virtual and located 20 cm from the lens
virtual and located about 6.67 cm from the lens, on the same side as the object
real and located 13.3 cm from the lens
questions.explanation: 1/v = 1/f - 1/u = -1/10 - 1/20 = -3/20, so v ≈ -6.67 cm. The negative sign shows a virtual image on the same side as the object, as expected for a diverging lens.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.text: In a resonance tube experiment (closed pipe), the first resonance occurs when the air column length is 17 cm, using a tuning fork of frequency 500 Hz. Neglecting end correction, calculate the speed of sound in air.
questions.explanation: For the first resonance in a closed pipe, the air column length equals a quarter wavelength: λ/4 = 17 cm, so λ = 68 cm = 0.68 m. Speed v = fλ = 500 x 0.68 = 340 m/s.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.text: An open pipe of length 0.5 m resonates at its fundamental frequency. If the speed of sound in air is 340 m/s, calculate the fundamental frequency.
questions.explanation: For an open pipe, the fundamental wavelength is λ = 2L = 1.0 m. Frequency f = v/λ = 340/1.0 = 340 Hz.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.text: A closed pipe of length 0.25 m resonates at its fundamental frequency, with the speed of sound in air being 340 m/s. Calculate the fundamental frequency.
questions.explanation: For a closed pipe, the fundamental wavelength is λ = 4L = 4 x 0.25 = 1.0 m. Frequency f = v/λ = 340/1.0 = 340 Hz.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.text: A car horn emits sound at 500 Hz as the car approaches a stationary observer at 34 m/s. If the speed of sound is 340 m/s, calculate the apparent frequency heard by the observer.
questions.explanation: For an approaching source, f' = f x v/(v - vs) = 500 x 340/(340-34) = 500 x 340/306 ≈ 555.6 Hz.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.text: Two tuning forks of frequencies 256 Hz and 260 Hz are sounded together. Calculate the beat frequency heard.
questions.explanation: Beat frequency equals the difference between the two frequencies: 260 - 256 = 4 Hz.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.text: The speed of sound in air at 0°C is 332 m/s and increases by about 0.6 m/s for every 1°C rise in temperature. Calculate the speed of sound at 25°C.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.text: A ship sends a sonar pulse that returns after 4 seconds. If the speed of sound in water is 1500 m/s, calculate the depth of the sea at that point.
questions.explanation: Total distance travelled by the pulse (down and back) = speed x time = 1500 x 4 = 6000 m, so depth = 6000/2 = 3000 m.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.text: Two point charges of +2 x 10⁻⁶ C and +3 x 10⁻⁶ C are separated by 0.3 m in air. Using k = 9 x 10⁹ Nm²/C², calculate the electrostatic force between them.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.text: Calculate the electric field intensity at a point 0.2 m from a point charge of 4 x 10⁻⁶ C in vacuum, given k = 9 x 10⁹ Nm²/C².

questions.subject: Physics
questions.text: A capacitor of capacitance 5 μF is connected to a 12 V battery. Calculate the charge stored on the capacitor.
questions.explanation: Charge Q = CV = 5μF x 12V = 60 μC.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.text: Calculate the energy stored in a 10 μF capacitor charged to a potential difference of 100 V.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.text: Resistors of 4 Ω and 6 Ω are connected in parallel, and this combination is connected in series with a 2 Ω resistor. Calculate the total resistance of the circuit.
questions.explanation: Parallel combination: (4x6)/(4+6) = 24/10 = 2.4 Ω. Adding the series resistor: total = 2.4 + 2 = 4.4 Ω.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.text: A circuit has a total resistance of 4.4 Ω and is connected to an 8.8 V battery. Calculate the total current drawn from the battery.
questions.explanation: By Ohm's Law, I = V/R = 8.8/4.4 = 2 A.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.text: A 12 Ω resistor carries a current of 3 A. Calculate the power dissipated in the resistor.
questions.explanation: Power P = I²R = 3² x 12 = 9 x 12 = 108 W.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.text: An electric heater rated 2000 W operates for 3 hours. Calculate the electrical energy consumed in kilowatt-hours.
questions.explanation: Energy = power x time = 2 kW x 3 h = 6 kWh.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.text: A battery of e.m.f. 12 V and internal resistance 0.5 Ω is connected to an external resistor of 5.5 Ω. Calculate the current flowing in the circuit.
questions.explanation: Total resistance = external + internal = 5.5 + 0.5 = 6.0 Ω. Current I = E/(R+r) = 12/6 = 2 A.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.text: A battery of e.m.f. 12 V and internal resistance 0.5 Ω delivers a current of 2 A through an external circuit. Calculate the terminal potential difference of the battery.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.text: Three identical cells, each of e.m.f. 1.5 V and internal resistance 0.2 Ω, are connected in series to an external resistor of 5.4 Ω. Calculate the current in the circuit.
questions.explanation: Total e.m.f. = 3 x 1.5 = 4.5 V. Total internal resistance = 3 x 0.2 = 0.6 Ω. Total resistance = 5.4 + 0.6 = 6.0 Ω. Current I = 4.5/6.0 = 0.75 A.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.text: Two identical cells, each of e.m.f. 2 V and internal resistance 1 Ω, are connected in parallel to an external resistance of 3 Ω. Calculate the current through the external resistor.
questions.explanation: For identical cells in parallel, the effective e.m.f. remains 2 V while the effective internal resistance is halved to 0.5 Ω. Total resistance = 3 + 0.5 = 3.5 Ω, so I = 2/3.5 ≈ 0.57 A.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.text: A wire of length 2 m and cross-sectional area 0.5 x 10⁻⁶ m² has a resistance of 4 Ω. Calculate the resistivity of the material.
questions.explanation: Resistivity ρ = RA/L = (4 x 0.5x10⁻⁶)/2 = (2x10⁻⁶)/2 = 1 x 10⁻⁶ Ω·m.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.text: Calculate the resistance of an electric bulb rated 60 W, 120 V.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.text: A straight conductor of length 0.5 m carrying a current of 4 A is placed perpendicular to a magnetic field of flux density 0.2 T. Calculate the force on the conductor.
questions.explanation: Force F = BIL = 0.2 x 4 x 0.5 = 0.4 N.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.text: A coil of 200 turns experiences a change in magnetic flux from 0.02 Wb to 0.05 Wb in 0.5 s. Calculate the average induced e.m.f.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.text: A step-up transformer has 100 turns on the primary coil and 500 turns on the secondary coil. If the primary voltage is 240 V, calculate the secondary voltage, assuming 100% efficiency.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.text: A transformer with primary voltage 240 V and secondary voltage 1200 V operates at 100% efficiency. If the secondary current is 2 A, calculate the primary current.
questions.explanation: By conservation of power (100% efficiency), VpIp = VsIs, so Ip = VsIs/Vp = (1200 x 2)/240 = 2400/240 = 10 A.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.text: Calculate the force experienced by an electron moving at 2 x 10⁶ m/s perpendicular to a magnetic field of flux density 0.5 T. (Charge on electron = 1.6 x 10⁻¹⁹ C)

questions.subject: Physics
questions.text: Lenz's Law states that the direction of an induced current is always such that it
options: aids the change in magnetic flux that produced it
is always in the same direction as the applied magnetic field
has no definite direction and varies randomly
opposes the change in magnetic flux that produced it
questions.explanation: Lenz's Law, a consequence of energy conservation, states that an induced current flows in a direction that opposes the very change in flux that generated it.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.text: The threshold frequency of a metal surface is 5 x 10¹⁴ Hz. Calculate the maximum kinetic energy of photoelectrons emitted when light of frequency 8 x 10¹⁴ Hz is incident on it. (h = 6.6 x 10⁻³⁴ Js)
questions.explanation: Maximum KE = h(f - f0) = 6.6x10⁻³⁴ x (8x10¹⁴ - 5x10¹⁴) = 6.6x10⁻³⁴ x 3x10¹⁴ = 1.98 x 10⁻¹⁹ J.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.text: A radioactive sample has a half-life of 8 days. Calculate the fraction of the original sample remaining after 24 days.
questions.explanation: Number of half-lives elapsed = 24/8 = 3. Fraction remaining = (1/2)³ = 1/8.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.text: A radioactive isotope has an initial mass of 80 g and a half-life of 10 years. Calculate the mass remaining after 40 years.
questions.explanation: Number of half-lives = 40/10 = 4. Remaining mass = 80 x (1/2)⁴ = 80/16 = 5 g.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.text: When a nucleus of uranium-238 (92 protons) emits an alpha particle, what are the atomic number and mass number of the resulting daughter nucleus?
questions.explanation: An alpha particle carries away 2 protons and a mass number of 4, so the daughter nucleus has atomic number 92-2=90 and mass number 238-4=234.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.text: In beta-minus decay, a neutron in the nucleus transforms into a proton with the emission of
options: an electron (beta particle) and an antineutrino
questions.explanation: Beta-minus decay converts a neutron into a proton, releasing a fast-moving electron (the beta particle) and an antineutrino to conserve energy and lepton number.
